meta.titre: Mineral Groups and Physical Properties: identifying minerals from structure, bonding and simple tests

sections.contenu_markdown: Imagine a student on a field trip in Cameroon who picks up a shiny, heavy mineral and, beside it, a soft, flaky one. With only a hand lens, a copper coin, a steel nail and a piece of unglazed tile she can name both. Minerals make up every rock, and the ores of iron, lead and other metals are minerals, so identifying them is the first skill of a working geologist. At the GCE you are asked to name the diagnostic property of a mineral group, to read a crystal drawing, and to explain how the way atoms are bonded decides hardness, cleavage and solubility.

items: Silicon and oxygen are the two most abundant elements in the Earth's crust.
Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds hold the particles of different solids together.
Density is mass divided by volume.
A crystal is a solid whose particles are arranged in a regular repeating pattern.

sections.titre: Mineral groups and physical properties: structure, tests and the effect of bonding
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What a mineral is
A **mineral** is a naturally occurring, inorganic, crystalline solid with a definite chemical composition (which may vary within limits) and an ordered atomic structure.

### Mineral groups
Silicates are built from the $\mathrm{SiO_4}$ tetrahedron and are grouped by how the tetrahedra are linked.

| Group | Linking | Examples and key properties |
|---|---|---|
| Nesosilicates | isolated tetrahedra | olivine, garnet: hard, no good cleavage |
| Inosilicates | single chains (pyroxene), double chains (amphibole) | two cleavages, near $90^\circ$ in pyroxene and near $56^\circ$ and $124^\circ$ in amphibole |
| Phyllosilicates | sheets | micas, chlorite, talc: one perfect cleavage, soft |
| Tectosilicates | three-dimensional framework | quartz (no cleavage, hardness 7), feldspars (two cleavages near $90^\circ$) |

Non-silicates include oxides (haematite $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$, magnetite $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$), sulphides (galena PbS, pyrite $\mathrm{FeS_2}$), carbonates (calcite $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$), sulphates (gypsum), halides (halite NaCl, fluorite $\mathrm{CaF_2}$) and native elements (gold, sulphur, graphite).

### Physical properties
- **Colour** varies with impurities and is unreliable; **streak**, the colour of the powder on unglazed porcelain, is constant.
- **Lustre**: metallic, vitreous, pearly, resinous, silky or earthy.
- **Hardness** is resistance to scratching, on **Mohs' scale**: 1 talc, 2 gypsum, 3 calcite, 4 fluorite, 5 apatite, 6 orthoclase, 7 quartz, 8 topaz, 9 corundum, 10 diamond. A fingernail is about 2.5, a copper coin about 3.5 and a steel nail about 5.5.
- **Cleavage** is breakage along planes of weak bonding, described by the number of directions and the angles between them; **fracture** is irregular breakage (conchoidal, splintery, uneven).
- **Specific gravity** is the density relative to water: $\mathrm{SG} = \dfrac{W_{\text{air}}}{W_{\text{air}} - W_{\text{water}}}$.
- **Habit** is the usual crystal shape (cubic, prismatic, acicular, fibrous, tabular, massive). Special tests include fizzing in dilute acid (calcite) and taste (halite).

### How bonding controls properties
- **Mica** has strong Si-O bonds inside its sheets but weak bonds between them, which gives one perfect cleavage and thin flexible flakes.
- **Quartz** has strong covalent bonds in all directions, so it is hard, has no cleavage and breaks with a conchoidal fracture.
- **Halite** is ionic: it cleaves along planes of the cubic lattice and dissolves because water molecules pull the ions out.
- **Native metals** have metallic bonding: they are malleable, conduct electricity and have a metallic lustre.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a crystal drawing is shown or the question asks for the crystal system or an example of a habit.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Describe the crystallographic axes first.

| System | Axes and angles | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Cubic | three equal axes at $90^\circ$ | halite, galena, pyrite |
| Tetragonal | two equal axes and one different, all at $90^\circ$ | zircon |
| Orthorhombic | three unequal axes, all at $90^\circ$ | olivine, barite |
| Monoclinic | three unequal axes, one angle not $90^\circ$ | gypsum, orthoclase, mica |
| Triclinic | three unequal axes, no angle $90^\circ$ | plagioclase feldspar |
| Hexagonal (with the trigonal division) | three equal horizontal axes at $120^\circ$ and a vertical axis | beryl, apatite, quartz |

A six-sided prism indicates the hexagonal division, for which beryl, apatite and quartz are examples.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a set of properties is given and the mineral must be named.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Work from the most reliable tests: lustre and streak, then hardness against the Mohs scale, then cleavage or fracture, then specific gravity, and finally a special test. Use a range for hardness (it scratches mineral A but is scratched by mineral B). Say which properties exclude the other candidates, not only which fit.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to explain a property in terms of structure and bonding.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use three links in each sentence: name the bond or structure, say what it allows, then state the property. For example: weak bonds between sheets mean the sheets part easily, so there is a perfect cleavage in one direction. Contrast two minerals where possible, such as hard quartz and soft talc.

sections.enonce_markdown: A specimen has a metallic lustre and a lead-grey streak. It is scratched by a copper coin; it scratches gypsum but does not scratch calcite. It breaks into small blocks with smooth faces that meet at $90^\circ$ in three directions. A piece weighs $75.0\ \mathrm{g}$ in air and $65.0\ \mathrm{g}$ when suspended in water. Identify the mineral and justify your answer.

etapes.justification: These are reliable and quick, and they separate metallic minerals such as sulphides and oxides from silicates with a glassy lustre.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A metallic lustre with a grey streak points to a sulphide or an oxide.

etapes.justification: Scratching a softer mineral and being scratched by a harder one gives a range on the Mohs scale.
etapes.resultat_markdown: It scratches gypsum (2) but not calcite (3), so the hardness is between 2 and 3, about 2.5.

etapes.justification: Three cleavages at right angles mean that the structure has cubic symmetry and that the weak planes lie along the cube faces.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Three cleavages at $90^\circ$ make cubic blocks, so the mineral crystallises in the cubic system.

etapes.justification: $\mathrm{SG} = W_{\text{air}} / (W_{\text{air}} - W_{\text{water}})$, because the loss of weight in water equals the weight of an equal volume of water.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $\mathrm{SG} = \dfrac{75.0}{75.0 - 65.0} = 7.5$, which is very high for a mineral that is not a native metal.

etapes.justification: The combination of metallic lustre, grey streak, low hardness, cubic cleavage and very high specific gravity fits a lead sulphide.
etapes.resultat_markdown: **Galena, PbS.** Halite is excluded because it has a vitreous lustre and an SG near 2.2; pyrite is harder (about 6).

sections.conclusion_markdown: The specimen is galena, PbS, the main ore of lead: a soft, heavy sulphide that cleaves into cubes along three directions at right angles.

items.erreur_markdown: "Colour is the best way to identify a mineral, so purple always means amethyst and quartz is always colourless."
items.pourquoi_faux: Colour changes with traces of impurities, so the same mineral can have many colours. Quartz is found colourless, purple, pink, smoky and in other colours.
items.correction_markdown: Use streak, hardness, cleavage or fracture and specific gravity, and use colour only as a hint.

items.erreur_markdown: "Cleavage surfaces and crystal faces are the same thing."
items.pourquoi_faux: Crystal faces are formed as the crystal grows; cleavage surfaces are formed when the mineral is broken along planes of weak bonding. Quartz has crystal faces but no cleavage.
items.correction_markdown: Define cleavage as breaking along planes of weakness, and describe the number of directions and the angles between them.

items.erreur_markdown: "Diamond is the hardest mineral, so it cannot be broken."
items.pourquoi_faux: Hardness is resistance to scratching, not resistance to breaking. A hard mineral can still split along a cleavage plane or shatter when struck.
items.correction_markdown: Say that diamond is the hardest mineral (10) but it can be cleaved; hardness and toughness are different.

items.erreur_markdown: "SG = 75.0 / 65.0 = 1.15" for a specimen weighing 75.0 g in air and 65.0 g in water.
items.pourquoi_faux: The denominator must be the loss of weight in water, which is the weight of the water displaced, not the weight in water.

items.erreur_markdown: "All silicate minerals have the same structure, so they have the same cleavage."
items.pourquoi_faux: Silicates differ in how the $\mathrm{SiO_4}$ tetrahedra are linked (isolated, chains, sheets or framework), and the pattern of strong and weak bonds controls cleavage.
items.correction_markdown: Link the structure to the property: sheets give one perfect cleavage (mica), a framework gives none (quartz).

items.enonce_markdown: (a) An unknown mineral scratches fluorite but is scratched by apatite. Between which two Mohs numbers does its hardness lie? (b) A crystal has three axes, two of them equal in length and one different, all meeting at $90^\circ$. State its crystal system. (c) Name the mineral group that splits into thin flexible sheets.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) It scratches fluorite (4), so the hardness is more than 4; apatite (5) scratches it, so the hardness is less than 5: **between 4 and 5**.

(b) Two equal axes and one different, all at right angles, is the **tetragonal** system.

(c) The **mica** group, which has one perfect cleavage because of weak bonds between its silicate sheets.

items.enonce_markdown: A fragment of an unknown mineral weighs $53.0\ \mathrm{g}$ in air and $33.0\ \mathrm{g}$ when suspended in water. (a) Calculate its specific gravity. (b) Decide which of quartz (SG 2.65), galena (SG 7.5) and halite (SG 2.2) it is. (c) Calculate the mass of a $40\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ piece of the same mineral.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathrm{SG} = \dfrac{53.0}{53.0 - 33.0} = \dfrac{53.0}{20.0} = $ **2.65**.

(b) The value matches **quartz**; it is too low for galena and clearly higher than halite.

(c) The density is $2.65\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, so the mass is $2.65\times40 = $ **$106\ \mathrm{g}$**.

items.enonce_markdown: Three unlabelled specimens are examined. A: vitreous and colourless, three cleavages at $90^\circ$, hardness 2.5, tastes salty and dissolves in water. B: white and vitreous, three cleavages not at $90^\circ$ that give rhombs, hardness 3, fizzes in cold dilute acid. C: glassy, no cleavage, conchoidal fracture, hardness 7, SG 2.65. (a) Name A, B and C. (b) Use bonding to explain why A dissolves in water and why C is much harder than A. (c) Name the crystal system of A.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) A is **halite**, B is **calcite** and C is **quartz**.

(b) Halite is ionic: water molecules are polar and attract the $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions out of the lattice, so it dissolves. Quartz is a framework of strong covalent Si-O bonds in every direction, which resists scratching and gives hardness 7, whereas the ionic bonding of halite is weaker and the mineral is soft (2.5).

(c) Halite crystallises in the **cubic** system.

items_markdown: A mineral is naturally occurring, inorganic, crystalline and of definite composition; silicates are grouped by how the $\mathrm{SiO_4}$ tetrahedra are linked.
Mica (a sheet silicate) has one perfect cleavage and splits into thin flexible flakes; quartz has no cleavage; pyroxene and amphibole show two cleavages at different angles.
Rely on streak, hardness, cleavage or fracture and specific gravity; colour is the least reliable property.
Hardness is resistance to scratching on Mohs' scale; cleavage is breakage along planes of weakness; the two must not be confused with toughness or crystal faces.
$\mathrm{SG} = W_{\text{air}}/(W_{\text{air}} - W_{\text{water}})$, and the denominator is the loss of weight in water.
Bonding decides properties: weak bonds give cleavage and softness, strong bonds in all directions give hardness, ionic solids can dissolve, metallic bonding gives malleability and conduction.
